Dear Diary,
Today was my 12th day in Chennai. Nobody at my new school knows my name yet except the teacher, and she says it wrong. At night the fan in my new room makes a different noise from our Lucknow fan, and I can hear the sea, which sounds like someone breathing. So I took my pillow to Mumma and Papa's room again. Papa said, "Eshaan, you're nine," but Mumma made space and said I'm still her big boy. I didn't make my bed today or feed the fish, even though that's my job. I don't know why. My brother Mridul fed them and didn't tell on me.
Tomorrow I will try to feed the fish.
Eshaan

qa.a: He didn't make his bed or feed the fish.

qa.a: Everything is new and strange, from the fan's noise to the sea, so being near his parents feels safe while he is stressed.

qa.q: What small step could help Eshaan feel settled at night?
qa.a: A parent could sit with him in his own room for a while, and he could feed the fish with someone, easing back into his old routines.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel when he feeds the fish for Eshaan?
qa.a: He might feel protective, noticing his brother is struggling, and not telling on him is a quiet kindness.

Uma's family had moved from the big city to a small town where Baba had taken a job at the sugar mill. The new house had a tin roof that rattled in the rain, and the school was two rooms and a banyan tree. Uma was eleven. She had always packed her own school bag and folded the clothes after they dried. Now her bag stayed wherever she dropped it, and the clothes sat in a heap on the charpai.
Every night she came to her parents' mat with her pillow. "Just tonight, Ma," she whispered, every night.
Her mother, Jaya, lifted the sheet and made room. "Just tonight," Jaya agreed, and stroked Uma's hair until the rain stopped.

qa.q: Where had Baba taken a job?
qa.a: At the sugar mill.

qa.q: Why might Uma keep whispering 'Just tonight, Ma' every night?
qa.a: She seems unsettled by the move and wants the comfort of her parents' mat, while also feeling a little embarrassed to need it at eleven.

qa.q: What choice of Jaya's helps, and what could she add later?
qa.a: Making room without scolding gives comfort; later she could bring back one small job, like folding clothes together, as Uma settles.

qa.q: How might Baba see Uma's return to their mat?
qa.a: He may feel responsible, since his new job caused the move, and want to give her time to adjust.

grounding: After a move to a small town, an eleven-year-old stops managing her usual chores and asks each night to sleep beside her parents.

Siddiq's family had moved from Cape Town to Johannesburg in July, in the middle of winter. At eight, he had always taken out the recycling and laid the table for supper without being asked. Now he forgot both, every day. And at night, after the lights were off, he padded down the corridor and curled up on the floor beside his parents' bed with his blanket. "The house makes noises," he said.
His mother didn't send him back. She put a camping mat there for him.
On Friday, a boy called Thabo from his new class asked him to play football at break. That night Siddiq fell asleep in his own bed for the first time since the move, still wearing his football socks.

qa.q: Where did Siddiq curl up at night?
qa.a: On the floor beside his parents' bed, with his blanket.

qa.q: What does 'The house makes noises' suggest Siddiq was feeling?
qa.a: He felt unsafe in the strange new house, and being near his parents brought back an earlier, simpler comfort.

qa.q: Which choice helped Siddiq most, and why?
qa.a: His mother's camping mat let him stay close without a fight, and a new friendship with Thabo gave him the confidence to go back to his own bed.

qa.q: What might Thabo's invitation have meant to Siddiq, even if Thabo didn't know it?
qa.a: It probably made Johannesburg feel less strange, giving Siddiq a friend and a reason to feel at home. 🙂

passage:
For the third morning running, Santosh, nine, sat in the sick room of his new Bengaluru school, holding his stomach. Nurse Hansa gave him warm water and sat beside him.
"Did you sleep okay?"
"On a mat," he said. "Next to Mummy and Papa's bed." In Patna he'd had his own room with a cricket poster. Here everything smelled of new paint, and he didn't know anyone's name at lunch.
"And who packs your bag?"
He looked at his shoes. "Mummy. I used to. I keep forgetting."
Hansa nodded. "Big moves make people want the old, cosy things for a while, even grown-ups. That's allowed. It usually settles."
Then she asked who he sat with at lunch, and wrote a note asking his class teacher to find him a buddy.

qa.q: Where does Santosh sleep now?
qa.a: On a mat, next to Mummy and Papa's bed.

qa.q: Why might sleeping near his parents feel right to Santosh now?
qa.a: Everything in Bengaluru is new and unsettling, so being close to Mummy and Papa brings back the safe feeling he had in Patna.

qa.q: What small step did Nurse Hansa take that could help Santosh settle?
qa.a: She wrote a note asking his class teacher to find him a lunch buddy, which targets the loneliness behind the stomach aches.

qa.q: How might Nurse Hansa see the three mornings in the sick room?
qa.a: Nurse Hansa seems to read the stomach aches as stress from the move rather than fuss, which is why the questions are about sleep, the bag and lunch.

grounding: Shows a child who has moved cities sleeping by his parents' bed and no longer packing his own bag, as the stress of the move pulls him back to early comforts.

passage:
I'm Gargi, Harsha's big sister, and since we moved from Mysuru to Delhi in June I've watched my brother turn about three years younger.
Back home, Harsha, ten, fed the fish every morning and watered Amma's tulsi without being asked. Here the fish tank goes cloudy until I notice. Every night he drags his old pillow into Amma and Appa's room and asks to sleep on the floor by their bed. Last week he even asked Amma to break his chapati for him.
I don't know exactly what's going on in his head. He says his new school is "fine". But when the winter fog came and he couldn't see the street from our balcony, he stood there a long time, very quiet.
Appa lets him stay. "For now," he told me. "He'll find his feet."

qa.q: What did Harsha do every morning back in Mysuru?
qa.a: He fed the fish and watered Amma's tulsi without being asked.

qa.q: Why might sleeping by his parents' bed comfort Harsha after the move?
qa.a: With a new city and a new school, being near Amma and Appa gives him the safety of being little again while everything else feels strange.

qa.q: How could the family help Harsha get back to his old jobs gently?
qa.a: They could keep letting him sleep nearby for now while handing back one familiar task, like feeding the fish together each morning, so the old routine returns step by step.

qa.q: How does Gargi feel about watching Harsha "turn three years younger"?
qa.a: Gargi seems puzzled and a little worried, noticing the cloudy tank and the quiet moments on the balcony, and cares enough to keep watching closely.

grounding: Illustrates, through an older sister's eyes, a child who has changed cities asking to sleep in the parents' room and dropping chores he used to manage.
